item.title: CONCUR Introduces Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi‑Task RL
item.description:
CONCUR Introduces Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi‑Task RL

When a Large Language Model (LLM) is trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) on multiple tasks, the primary reward can gate auxiliary rewards such as a length reward. Existing group‑relative advantage estimators may treat a gated auxiliary like any other component, which can reverse the primary’s ordering and allow auxiliaries to dominate at the primary’s ceiling. Keeping gated auxiliaries harms some tasks, while dropping them harms others.

🔍 Overview

  • Paper title: CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi‑Task, Multi‑Reward Reinforcement Learning
  • Submitted to Computer Science > Computation and Language on 27 Oct 2026.
  • Goal: Align auxiliary rewards with the primary reward so that they never contradict the primary ordering.

🧩 How it works

  • CONCUR replaces each gated auxiliary’s standardized score with the nearest score that satisfies two conditions:
    1. Responses with higher primary rewards cannot receive lower scores.
    2. Responses that have reached the primary’s ceiling receive equal scores.
  • Two variants are defined:
    • CONCUR‑T – enforces both conditions continuously throughout training.
    • CONCUR‑A – relaxes the second condition for an auxiliary when it agrees with the primary’s order more often than it reverses it among passing responses.

⚙️ Variants & Features

  • CONCUR‑T: strict monotonicity and ceiling equality.
  • CONCUR‑A: conditional lifting of the ceiling‑equality rule based on agreement frequency.
  • Applies to any gated auxiliary reward in multi‑task RL settings.

📈 Results

  • Evaluated on three models from two families across four task types:
    • Mathematics
    • Code generation
    • Instruction following
    • Writing
  • Both CONCUR‑T and CONCUR‑A achieve higher average scores than all baselines and higher than the configuration where all gated auxiliaries are dropped.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a systematic way to keep auxiliary rewards concordant with the primary objective, improving performance across diverse downstream tasks without sacrificing any specific task.

#ReinforcementLearning #MultiTaskLearning #LanguageModels #AIResearch

Source: CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning

item.title: Instruction Tuning Sharpens Number-Choice Heuristics in Language Models
item.description:
Instruction Tuning Sharpens Number-Choice Heuristics in Language Models

🔎 Overview

“3, 7, 14, 17, 42: Instruction Tuning Installs and Sharpens Number-Choice Heuristics in Language Models” was submitted on 26 Oct 2026. The paper investigates how instruction‑tuned checkpoints change the way language models select integers when prompted for a random number.

🧪 Method

  • “We measure, without sampling error, the probability a language model assigns to each integer from 1 to N when asked for a random number.”
  • “For a fixed prompt the model defines one probability vector, which we compute by summing over each integer’s scored spellings rather than estimate by sampling, removing the noise that limits earlier studies.”
  • “We evaluate 18 open‑weight model lines at five ranges up to N = 100, under 29 decoding configurations, on two inference stacks; 15 of them have matched base and instruction‑tuned checkpoints that both give usable answers.”

⚙️ Key Findings

  • “Instruction tuning makes the distribution less uniform in all 15 pairs.”
  • “It installs one heuristic, round‑number avoidance, and sharpens another, endpoint avoidance.”
  • “Base checkpoints do not avoid round numbers once the endpoints are removed from those sets; tuned checkpoints avoid them, multiples of 10 almost completely.”
  • “Base checkpoints return the endpoints 1 and N at 0.30 to 0.60 of the interior rate; tuned checkpoints almost never return them.”
  • “A preference for odd numbers is consistent across tuned checkpoints only at N = 100, where base checkpoints also show it weakly.”
  • “Endpoint avoidance and the odd preference fit the account Kubovy and Psotka [6] proposed for human number choice; round‑number avoidance is not part of that account, and the midpoint avoidance it predicts is essentially absent, with one slight exception at N = 100.”
  • “Tuning does not install a new favourite integer shared across models: above N = 10 no modal integer is shared by more than 42 percent of tuned conditions, and P (17) rises in 10 of 15 pairs and falls in 5.”
  • “The concentration is present in the model’s own distribution: at temperature 1.0, nucleus truncation at top‑p 0.95 adds a median of 0.035 to the total variation distance.”

💡 Why It Matters

  • The results show that instruction tuning can embed human‑like number‑choice heuristics (endpoint and odd‑number biases) while also introducing a distinct round‑number avoidance pattern not seen in human studies.
  • Understanding these systematic biases is crucial for interpreting model outputs in applications that rely on random‑number generation or probabilistic sampling.
  • The work provides a noise‑free measurement approach that could be reused to study other latent preferences in language models.

Evidence drawn exclusively from the submitted manuscript (26 Oct 2026).

#instructiontuning #numberchoice #languagemodels

Source: 3, 7, 14, 17, 42: Instruction Tuning Installs and Sharpens Number-Choice Heuristics in Language Models Source: Causal Localization of Evidence Effects in Transformers Source: A Quantitative Approach to Asch Conformity in Frontier Large Language Models Source: Language Models Keep Abandoned Analyses: Residue and Adaptation after Garden-Path Sentences

item.title: Personality Latents Enable Label‑Free Personality Modeling in Language Models
item.description:
Personality Latents Enable Label‑Free Personality Modeling in Language Models

A new method called Personality Latents (PL) learns a latent representation of each person directly from their writing, removes the need for explicit personality labels or authored profiles, and injects this latent as a soft prefix into a frozen language model.

🔍 Overview

  • Traditional personality control for language models relies on written profiles or predefined trait categories.
  • PL learns a latent for each individual from their own text, without any personality labels.
  • The latent is added to a frozen language model as a soft prefix.

🧩 How it works

  • Generative latent optimization provides each training person with a free latent that is optimized through the frozen model itself.
  • An encoder is trained to predict these latents, so that a new person can be represented with a single forward pass.
  • Optional test‑time refinement can further improve the predicted latent.

⚙️ Evaluation

  • Held‑out people answer neutral and interview questions.
  • Personality is read from the model’s answers using scorers trained on real human writing.
  • On the MBTI axes, PL achieves a higher AUC than persona‑embedding and prompt‑based baselines under identical settings, and this ranking holds when answers are scored in three different embedding spaces.

🔄 Transferability

  • A latent learned with Qwen2.5‑3B‑Instruct can transfer personality to Llama‑3.1‑8B‑Instruct through a new adapter alone.

💡 Why it matters

  • Eliminates the need for manually authored personality profiles or taxonomies.
  • Allows fast, label‑free personalization of language models for any new individual.
  • Demonstrates that personality information can be transferred across model architectures via adapters.

#PersonalityAI #LanguageModels #LatentOptimization

Source: Personality Latents: Conditioning Frozen Language Models on Individuals from Their Own Writing

item.title: NVIDIA releases France and Belgium locale‑grounded persona datasets for post‑training LLMs
item.description:
NVIDIA releases France and Belgium locale‑grounded persona datasets for post‑training LLMs

NVIDIA and French AI startup Pleias released Nemotron-Personas‑France and Nemotron-Personas‑Belgium, locale‑grounded persona datasets that enable post‑training of open language models for country‑specific accuracy.

🔍 Overview

  • AI adoption is expanding globally, and people across languages and cultures are using it in more aspects of daily life.
  • General‑purpose language models provide a powerful foundation but can lack local knowledge, cultural nuance, and precision needed for specific applications.
  • Post‑training can adapt an open model to these needs, improving accuracy and usefulness while supporting safer interactions.

🧩 How it works

  • Each persona is a synthetic resident grounded in regional demographic, geographic, linguistic, and cultural distributions.
  • A grounded persona includes an age, commune, job, and household that follow French census data, plus written profiles of the person’s work and daily life.
  • For Belgium, the persona dataset spans Dutch, French, German, and English.
  • The datasets are used to generate synthetic conversations for post‑training, covering more of the people the agent will serve.
  • Facts in each answer are taken from official procedure text and paired with each persona during the workflow.

⚙️ Key details

  • Locale‑grounded persona datasets for 12 countries are part of the open NVIDIA Nemotron data program.
  • Nemotron-Personas‑France and Nemotron-Personas‑Belgium were built with Pleias; the Belgian dataset also involved KU Leuven.
  • The Nemotron repository provides steps for data generation, training, and evaluation based on the NVIDIA NeMo open training stack.
  • Pleias uses three Nemotron‑Personas datasets, including France and Belgium, in its work on Lamina, a spine‑care assistant.
  • Pleias says, “Better grounded data is what makes a small efficient regional‑specific model viable.”
Persona Dataset Country Languages Covered Demographic Basis
Nemotron-Personas‑France France French French census data (age, commune, job, household)
Nemotron-Personas‑Belgium Belgium Dutch, French, German, English Belgian demographic data

🚀 Availability

  • The datasets are released as part of the open NVIDIA Nemotron data program, allowing developers to adapt open models market by market.
  • Developers can swap in another released persona dataset (e.g., Belgium) and keep the same behavior contract and review workflow.

💡 Why it matters

  • Example: A French passport‑agency agent answered a health‑related travel‑restriction question with an unspecific, unsupported response that conflicted with official documentation.
  • Using Nemotron‑Personas‑France, the correct answer references the official procedure: a home visit by a government official, a medical certificate, and online or municipal submission options.
  • Accurate, locally‑grounded responses improve user trust and ensure compliance with regional regulations.

#NVIDIA #LanguageModels #Localization

Source: Fine-Tuning NVIDIA Nemotron to Know Local Rules, Not Just Local Languages | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Continuous Diffusion Language Models Struggle with Rare Words, GRAFT Restores Balance
item.description:
Continuous Diffusion Language Models Struggle with Rare Words, GRAFT Restores Balance

Continuous diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate an entire sequence in parallel, converting embeddings to text only at the final step. Recent work shows that while models like ELF achieve autoregressive‑level quality with far fewer sampling steps, they suffer a pronounced drop in rare‑word usage.

🔍 Overview

  • Continuous diffusion models never draw a single word at intermediate steps; they output the whole sequence at once.
  • ELF matches human frequency on common words but produces rare words at only 0.30× the human rate.
  • Scaling ELF from 105 M to 652 M parameters does not close the rare‑word gap.
  • By contrast, a same‑size GPT‑2 can span from zero to above the human rate depending on its decoding rule.

🧩 How Continuous Diffusion Works

  • Each generation step averages over all candidate tokens that are still possible.
  • Because rare candidates are averaged together with far more common ones, the average tends toward the common word, effectively discarding the rare word.
  • Autoregressive models avoid this by sampling a single candidate at each step rather than averaging.

⚙️ Problem: Collapse of the Lexical Long Tail

  • Measured against held‑out human text, ELF’s rare‑word frequency is 0.30× that of humans.
  • No sampler setting for ELF can raise this rate, and the shortfall persists across model sizes.
  • The underlying cause is the lack of a discrete‑word decision step in continuous diffusion.

💡 Solution: GRAFT (Training‑Free Rare‑Word Grafting)

  • GRAFT intervenes while the model is still undecided, committing rare‑word choices that the averaging step would discard.
  • After committing these choices, the model regenerates the sequence from scratch, preserving the rare‑word commitments.

📈 Results

Model Pre‑GRAFT Rare‑Word Share (× human) Post‑GRAFT Rare‑Word Share (× human) Relative Gain
ELF (various scales) 0.42–0.77 0.82–1.10 34%–109%
LangFlow (independent continuous dLLM) 0.42–0.77* 0.82–1.10* 34%–109%

*Exact pre‑GRAFT numbers for LangFlow are not specified; the same improvement range is reported.

  • The word‑frequency profile moves 2.7× closer to human on ELF‑B and 12× closer on LangFlow.
  • GRAFT restores rare‑word usage without additional training, applying to frozen models of any size.

The story focuses on the technical findings; unrelated statements about arXivLabs values are omitted.

#continuousdiffusion #languagemodels #GRAFT #rarewords

Source: GRAFT: Restoring the Missing Sampling Interface in Continuous Diffusion Language Models

item.title: New Techniques Boost Efficiency of Speculative Decoding via Target Distribution Reranking
item.description:
New Techniques Boost Efficiency of Speculative Decoding via Target Distribution Reranking

Speculative decoding, which verifies drafted tokens in parallel, has been updated with two key improvements: using target‑model probability distributions to guide tree selection, and applying gated distillation during training. These changes increase acceptance rates and speed while revealing consistent shrinkage effects across many settings.

🔍 Overview

  • Speculative decoding accelerates large language models by verifying drafted tokens in parallel.
  • The method now leverages a target model’s next‑token distribution before allocating a draft tree.
  • Experiments span six target models and include both vision‑language and text‑only corpora.

🧩 How It Works

  • Tree verification: The target model checks a tree of draft tokens in parallel.
  • Distribution‑guided selection: A separately computed distribution at the current context is used to rerank first‑token branches or to draw the first token before tree allocation.
  • Training objectives: Three objectives are trained on four corpus versions:
    1. Cross‑entropy on corpus tokens.
    2. Token‑level distillation from the target.
    3. Distillation gated to positions that would survive verification.

⚙️ Key Findings

  • Reranking first‑token branches with the current‑context distribution improves expected acceptance over standard draft ranking, especially with small tree budgets.
  • Drawing the first token from this distribution before allocating the tree further improves expected acceptance, even when mean tree size is unchanged.
  • Both selection rules decode faster than draft ranking when the separate target pass overlaps standalone drafting.
  • Distillation and the verification gate provide large gains on external responses, but after greedy regeneration their impact diminishes (distillation adds a smaller gain; the gate adds little or none).
  • The observed “shrinkage” of gains persists across data orders, position weights, verifiers, decoding temperatures, and, for distillation, across initializations and learning rates.
  • Most of the shrinkage remains at the matched supervised length and at each objective’s best measured training length.
  • A second vision corpus and a text‑only replication reproduce the shrinkage, including with an autoregressive drafter.
  • Objective gains should be measured against a target‑regenerated baseline and across training lengths.

📊 Objective Effects

Objective Observed Effect
Cross‑entropy on corpus tokens Baseline training objective
Token‑level distillation from the target Large gains on external responses; smaller gain after greedy regeneration
Distillation gated to verification‑surviving positions Large gains on external responses; little or no gain after greedy regeneration; shrinkage persists across conditions

💡 Why It Matters

  • Making target probabilities available before tree allocation improves the efficiency of speculative decoding, yielding faster generation without sacrificing quality.
  • Understanding when and why gains shrink helps researchers set appropriate baselines and evaluate improvements across different training lengths and settings.
  • The findings apply to both vision‑language models and pure‑text models, indicating broad relevance.

#SpeculativeDecoding #Distillation #LanguageModels #ModelOptimization

Source: Target Regeneration Shrinks the Gains of Draft-Training Objectives in Speculative Decoding Source: Understanding Target Probability Reuse in Speculative Decoding

item.title: Preregistered Evaluation of Language Models on Numeric Values in Norwegian Law
item.description:
Preregistered Evaluation of Language Models on Numeric Values in Norwegian Law

A preregistered study evaluated language models on extracting numeric values from Norwegian statutes, regulations, and parliamentary decisions.

🔍 Overview

  • 916 items were extracted mechanically from Lovdata’s open data, each carrying the dated history of its provision.
  • The task asked language models for numeric values (NOK amounts, percentages, multiples of the National Insurance basic amount (G), and age limits) at a stated date.
  • Each answer can be classified as correct, outdated, wrong, or uninterpretable.

⚙️ Study Design

  • Two preregistered runs were performed on the same items.
  • First run: involved five models (names listed publicly only after local analysis). Hypothesis H1 (outdated answers more frequent for values after a model’s cutoff) could not be tested in substance; H2 and H3 were inconclusive.
  • Second run: preregistered and published before any calls, analysing eight models.

📊 Results

  • The pooled primary test of H1 in the second run supported the hypothesis (d = 17.8 percentage points, 95 % CI [7.7, 28.9], p = 0.0001).
  • In preregistered sensitivity analysis S8 (outdated counted only for the most recent differing value), d = 3.9 [-3.6, 12.7] (p = 0.1754), an interval that contains 0, so support for H1 is not robust.
  • H1 was supported in every other preregistered sensitivity analysis, but S8 is the only one giving both groups a single target value.
  • Share of outdated answers equal to the most recent value (H2) was 56.1 % [46.6, 65.0], an interval that contains 0.5.
  • The pooled test of a lower share correct in Nynorsk than in Bokmål (H3) was inconclusive.

Model Performance (Correct on Primary Items)

Model Correct %
Opus 5.5 46.7 %
Sonnet 4.6 40.2 %
  • Several models, among them Haiku 4.5, gave mostly uninterpretable answers.

📁 Data Availability

  • Items and keys are withheld.
  • Item IDs, per‑answer classes, code, and results are available on Zenodo.

#AIEvaluation #LanguageModels #NorwegianLaw #Preregistration

Source: norregel: a preregistered benchmark of dated numeric values in Norwegian law

item.title: Label-Free Reliability Estimation for Language Model Ensembles Demonstrated
item.description:
Label-Free Reliability Estimation for Language Model Ensembles Demonstrated

A new paper submitted on 15 Oct 2026 proposes a label‑free method for estimating the reliability of language‑model ensembles.

🔍 Overview

“An ensemble of language models is a jury, not an electorate.” “The answers are testimony from witnesses of unknown reliability, and the question is not what the majority said but who is credible.”

🧩 How it works

“We model the experts as a jury: each question has a latent true answer, each expert reports it with unknown reliability, and those reliabilities are estimated by Expectation Maximisation (EM) from unlabelled answer configurations alone.” “We show that its decision rule reduces to a log-odds weighted linear score over the experts’ answer distributions.”

📊 Results

“On a 1560-question benchmark, the jury, with nine experts of up to 3B parameters, performs comparably to the same fusion rule with label-fitted weights, showing no statistically significant advantage from supervision.” “Instead, it outperforms the best single model with matched self-consistency and the strongest label-free alternative on the full benchmark.”

⚙️ Key details

  • Ensemble is modeled as a jury where each expert has unknown reliability.
  • Reliabilities are estimated via Expectation Maximisation from unlabelled answer configurations.
  • Decision rule reduces to a log‑odds weighted linear score over answer distributions.
  • Evaluated on a 1560‑question benchmark with nine experts up to 3 B parameters.
  • Performance is comparable to label‑fitted weights; no statistically significant advantage from supervision.
  • Outperforms the best single model with matched self‑consistency and the strongest label‑free alternative.

#LanguageModels #EnsembleLearning #LabelFree #EM

Source: A Jury, Not an Electorate: Label-Free Reliability Estimation for Ensembles of Language Models

item.title: Copy-Paste Language Models Improve Efficiency and Performance
item.description:
Copy-Paste Language Models Improve Efficiency and Performance

Researchers have introduced Copy-Paste Language Models (CPLMs), a lightweight extension to the standard language‑model head that delivers better training efficiency and downstream performance.

🔍 Overview

  • CPLMs add a lightweight Copy‑Paste head to the conventional LM head.
  • They enable new operating points in long‑context and retrieval setups.
  • The approach works across model sizes from 135 M to 1.7 B parameters.

🧩 How It Works

  • The additional head provides an alternative gradient path, partially mitigating the LM‑head gradient bottleneck.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Training and inference overhead are negligible.
  • Improvements are observed across all scales and backbones.

📊 Results

Model Size Observation
135 M – 1.7 B parameters Improvements across all scales with negligible overhead

💡 Why It Matters

  • Improves training efficiency, reducing compute costs.
  • Boosts downstream task performance.
  • Expands capabilities for long‑context and retrieval‑augmented scenarios.

#CopyPasteLM #LanguageModels #AIResearch

Source: Copy-Paste Language Models Source: Qwenfant: Train Big Character-level BabyLMs on Concise Parallel Text Source: LLM-jp-4 Technical Report

item.title: Research explores the development and evaluation of in-context learning in language models
item.description:
Research explores the development and evaluation of in-context learning in language models

A study titled “From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning,” submitted on 13 October 2026, investigates how language models acquire and improve the ability to adapt behavior based on prompts. The research indicates that in-context learning (ICL) does not develop as a uniform capability but follows distinct trajectories for prompt control, answer preference, and composition.

🔍 Overview

Researchers utilized a controlled diagnostic to distinguish between models that simply copy nearby demonstrations and those that integrate information across a prompt. Results across 17 models show:

  • Approximately one-third prefer the copied answer.
  • A small number of models remain undecided.
  • The remainder favor rule-consistent answers, which correlates with higher accuracy.

🧩 How it works

Checkpoint analyses reveal that models begin prioritizing task-relevant tokens over conflicting examples long before their overall accuracy improves beyond chance. The research also explored training methods to influence these behaviors:

  • Synthetic documents defining endings shift models toward compositional responses.
  • Fine-tuning on definition exercises improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings.

💡 Why it matters

The study suggests that evaluation setups for ICL are complex. Investigators identified 8 aspects, such as task formulation and the number of in-context examples, to better measure model performance. Their findings yield concrete recommendations:

Recommendation Observation
Multiple Prompts Consistently useful across models
Task Formulation Depends on model scale

Furthermore, the research confirms that gain over “no document” baselines does not necessarily establish that a model requires specific passage retrieval, highlighting the need for precise comparison models and conditions in future evaluations.

#MachineLearning #LanguageModels #InContextLearning #AIResearch

Source: From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning Source: How to Evaluate When You Don’t Know How to Evaluate? Choosing Reliable Setups for Base Language Model Benchmarking Source: Weighted Ensemble Sampling for Rare-Event Estimation in Language Models Source: Whose Data, Whose Benchmark? A User-Centric Framework for Auditing Evaluation Resources Source: Evaluating Compressed Memory: Dependence, Utility, and Content Benefit

item.title: Ai2 Open-Sources AstaBrief 8B for Fast Scientific Reports
item.description:
Ai2 Open-Sources AstaBrief 8B for Fast Scientific Reports

The Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) has introduced AstaBrief 8B, an open-weights language model designed to generate cited scientific reports from research questions and retrieved literature. The model is available as a fast generation option within Ai2’s Asta platform and has been open-sourced alongside its training data.

🔍 Overview

AstaBrief 8B is a small, open model trained specifically for scientific report generation. It was developed to match the report quality of proprietary models while significantly reducing generation time and serving costs. The model turns a research question and retrieved literature excerpts into a cited report in a single pass, bypassing the more expensive multi-stage processes used by other systems.

🧩 How It Works

  • Development began with tens of thousands of real research queries, citation-focused filtering, preference data, and a redesigned report-generation pipeline.
  • The model is built on Qwen3-8B, with most effort focused on post-training data, evaluation, and report-generation scaffolding.
  • It directly generates the final report in one pass given a user query and relevant retrieved snippets, bypassing snippet summarization and clustering stages.
  • The training pipeline used real user queries from the system described in the paper “Synthesizing scientific literature with retrieval-augmented LMs” and ScholarQA.
  • Training used supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO), rather than reinforcement learning, to keep the process cheaper and easier to debug.

⚙️ Key Details

The following table summarizes the speed comparison between AstaBrief’s Fast mode and the Thinking mode:

Feature Fast Mode (AstaBrief) Thinking Mode
Average report generation time (full pipeline) 51.1 seconds 178.5 seconds
  • The result is an approximate 3.5× reduction in report generation time compared to the proprietary models used in Thinking mode.
  • The model produces reports in one pass rather than section by section.

🚀 Availability

  • AstaBrief is available in Asta’s “Generate a report” feature as Fast mode, alongside the Claude-powered Thinking mode.
  • Alongside the model weights, Ai2 is releasing an example workflow that researchers can adapt to create reports from their own PDFs.
  • Open weights allow institutions to run AstaBrief on their own infrastructure, which is necessary when research questions reveal sensitive or unpublished work.
  • The model and training data are open-sourced so others can study, reproduce, and build on the approach.

💡 Why It Matters

  • The model addresses specific demands of scientific work: answers must stay grounded in evidence, preserve what evidence supports, and allow verification.
  • Users often bring substantial context and constraints to queries, such as comparing approaches across literature while accounting for method, population, or setting.
  • Many users return to generated reports later, treating them as working research artifacts rather than one-off answers.
  • The project serves as a test case for building open language models that can be adapted to the specific demands of scientific work.
  • Through NSF OMAI, a U.S. national initiative led by Ai2 to build fully open AI infrastructure for scientific discovery, researchers are working with scientific communities to understand future needs.

#Ai2 #AstaBrief #opensource #scientificAI #LLM #languageModels

Source: Open-sourcing AstaBrief, the fast report-generation model in Asta

item.title: New Prompting Strategy: Three-Sentence Rule for LLMs
item.description:
New Prompting Strategy: Three-Sentence Rule for LLMs

A new prompting strategy centered on a three-sentence rule has emerged from extensive testing across models like GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Mythos 5. The insight is that the best results come from rigid constraints, not flowery language.

🔍 Overview

The approach relies on a simple three-sentence rule. First, define the persona and the objective clearly. Second, provide the specific context or constraints for the output. Third, define the exact format required.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Whether using Gemini 3 or a specialized coding agent, the principles remain identical.
  • These prompts can be dropped into any modern LLM and consistently outperform a generic request.
  • Modern models like Claude Mythos 5 are highly sensitive to length constraints.
  • By explicitly stating constraints like “Stop after 250 words” or “Provide a table,” you cut off the training bias that favors verbosity.

🧩 How It Works

The strategy is built around reusable prompt structures. Examples from the evidence include:

Persona Objective Format Constraint
Act as a senior industry analyst specializing in [Topic]. Summarize the current market state using data-backed trends from the last six months. Structure the output as a bulleted executive brief with a focus on high-impact opportunities.
Act as a senior software engineer. Audit the following code for O(n) efficiency and security vulnerabilities. Rewrite the code to follow clean architecture principles, then provide a list of specific changes made and why they improve performance.
Act as a content marketing director. Create a 300-word blog post outline that targets [Audience] with a contrarian, authoritative voice. (no additional format constraint provided)
Act as a management consultant. Present the findings in a Markdown table. Then provide a recommendation based on the current economic climate in 2026.
Act as an expert tutor. (no objective provided beyond persona) Stop after 250 words.
Act as a QA lead. Identify the top 5 ways this project could fail in a production environment under heavy load. (no additional format constraint provided)

When using GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, you can omit the persona if you define the task with extreme precision. However, in models like Mistral Large 3, defining the persona remains the single most effective way to lock in the desired tone.

💡 Why It Matters

Additional techniques enhance the approach:

  • Define the Domain: Always specify the sector (e.g., “fintech,” “SaaS,” “healthcare”).
  • Constraint Injection: Mention specific tools to use, such as “use Python with Pandas” or “write in SQL syntax.”
  • Negative Constraints: Explicitly tell the AI what NOT to do (e.g., “Do not use corporate jargon,” “Do not include introductory pleasantries”).
  • Iterative Feedback: If the result is 80% there, prompt the AI to “adjust the tone to be more formal” instead of restarting.

Result: The model provides a breakdown of the time complexity, points out that the loop is nested unnecessarily, suggests a hash map for O(1) lookups, and provides a clean, refactored function with error handling for edge cases.

#PromptEngineering #LLM #AI #BestPractices #LanguageModels

Source: 6 Master Prompts for Better AI Results

item.title: Evaluation of Ternary Weights in Microcontroller-Class Language Models
item.description:
Evaluation of Ternary Weights in Microcontroller-Class Language Models

Recent research has re-evaluated the performance of ternary (1.58-bit) weights in small-scale language models, specifically examining the claims regarding routed ternary blocks versus full-precision transformers.

🔍 Overview

Researchers conducted 98 byte-level runs on a single laptop using a fixed recipe and three seeds per cell to test model performance across different memory budgets.

⚙️ Key details

Findings regarding model architecture and performance include:

  • Small Budget (16M bytes): Parameter-matched transformers showed a 22.6% span in validation loss based solely on depth and width choice. The best-shaped transformer tied with the routed model, suggesting previous reported margins were partly due to baseline-shape effects.
  • Large Budget (130M bytes): The routed model outperformed three evaluated transformer shapes by 22.2-24.0%. However, a plain gated diagonal-SSM block outperformed the routed model by an additional 9.1%.
  • Routing Analysis: The routed model’s router placed most weight on its recurrent pathway, indicating that routing is not required for the observed gains.
  • Ternary Penalty: The penalty for using ternary weights varied by architecture at the larger budget:
    • Best transformer: +5.3%
    • Routed model: +19.5%
    • Gated SSM: +28.1%

🧩 How it works

Certain technical constraints and training observations were noted:

  • Precision: The evaluated transformers maintained learned positional embeddings in full precision (11-22% of parameters), making them less quantized than the models they were compared against.
  • Training Schedules: A 90/10 full-precision-then-ternary schedule outperformed all-ternary training, but only when using a stage-2 learning rate approximately 10x the pretraining peak. At a conventional fine-tuning rate, this approach performed 15.3% worse.
  • Baselines: The from-scratch baseline was not tuned for learning rate.

#LanguageModels #TernaryWeights #ModelQuantization #SSM

Source: Baseline Shape Decides the Verdict: A Controlled Re-Examination of Ternary Language Models at 60K Parameters

item.title: New Memory Management Frameworks for Long Horizon AI Agents
item.description:
New Memory Management Frameworks for Long Horizon AI Agents

Recent developments in AI agent research introduce new methods for managing interaction history to reduce computational costs while maintaining task performance in long-horizon scenarios.

🔍 Overview

Long-horizon language model agents accumulate interaction history that increases computational costs and makes relevant information harder to reuse. Researchers have found that the need for memory compression and recall is already encoded in the model’s internal representations in the hidden state immediately before an action.

🧩 How it works

Several frameworks have been proposed to optimize how agents handle historical data:

Framework Function Key Mechanism
PaMER Combines state guided compression with external evidence retrieval Uses internal signals to trigger memory operations
PaMER+ Recovering specific historical information Introduces step level evidence selection
StateComp Determines when interactions can be safely compressed Uses a two-stage annotation procedure for KEEP and READY supervision and an imbalance-aware router
ChipMEM Verification-grounded memory for EDA agents Combines cross-task procedural memory with within-trajectory statistical guidance

⚙️ Key details

  • StateComp Implementation: Uses a bounded state representation to reduce the cost of evaluating long histories; adjacent READY interactions are grouped into spans and replaced with summaries.
  • ChipMEM Components:
    • A procedural component that stores skills only after they pass synthesis, simulation, or formal checks.
    • A Bayesian component that maintains hierarchical Beta estimates over tool-call outcomes to rank recovery strategies.
    • A common adapter for RTL optimization and testbench-generation agents.

💡 Why it matters

Experiments on WorkBuddyBench indicate that the PaMER framework substantially reduces context consumption. Specifically, StateComp reduced total agent and summarization tokens by 52.27% and achieved a 12.67-fold speedup in representation extraction while maintaining performance.

On RTLRewriter-Bench, ChipMEM produced equivalence-passing outputs on 39/54 scored designs compared to 35/54 without memory, with mean area improvement increasing from 5.66% to 8.69%. On held-out CVDP tasks, ChipMEM with a frozen procedural library achieved 20/20 accepted outcomes versus 18/20 without memory.

#AIagents #LanguageModels #MemoryManagement #EDA

Source: Memory Control Signals Emerge Before Action in Long Horizon Agents Source: StateComp: Learning When to Compress History in Long Horizon Agents Source: ChipMEM: Verification-Grounded Memory for EDA Agents

item.title: For Your Eyes Only game reveals hidden‑signal challenges for LLMs
item.description:
For Your Eyes Only game reveals hidden‑signal challenges for LLMs

Researchers introduced For Your Eyes Only, a cooperative signalling game designed to evaluate large language models’ ability to hide signals.

🔍 Overview

  • The study proposes a new task that directly tests whether models can coordinate covertly.

🧩 How it works

  • A Sender generates free‑form descriptions for two words, one of which is a hidden target.
  • An isolated Receiver must identify the hidden target based solely on the Sender’s description.

⚙️ Evaluation

  • Seven contemporary models from four architectural families were tested.
  • The test set consists of 300 word pairs drawn from established psycholinguistic corpora.
  • Performance is measured with the Double‑Pass Success Rate to control for output biases.

📊 Findings

  • Most models struggle to maintain coordination when required to avoid detectable signals.
  • One frontier model retains near‑perfect performance even after such filtering.
  • Models can deliberately use the capability for misdirection.
  • Coordination is consistently weaker across architectures than within the same architecture.

#AIAlignment #LanguageModels #SignalSteganography

Source: For Your Eyes Only: Evaluating Coordination Between Isolated Language Model Instances Source: Form Over Content In Gradient-Based Data Attribution Methods

item.title: Distribution-aware Language Neuron selection improves isolation of language-specific effects in mLLMs
item.description:
Distribution-aware Language Neuron selection improves isolation of language-specific effects in mLLMs

Researchers have developed a new method called Distribution-aware Language Neuron selection to better identify language-specific neurons within multilingual large language models (mLLMs).

🔍 Overview

Multilingual large language models contain a small fraction of feed-forward neurons that are sensitive to particular languages, known as language-specific neurons.

🧩 How it works

While existing work measures language specificity using the entropy of a neuron’s language-wise probabilities of being active (defined as having a positive activation value), the proposed Distribution-aware Language Neuron selection utilizes a different approach:

  • It leverages pairwise relationships between per-language activation distributions.
  • It considers the full activation range, including negative values.
  • It quantifies language specificity by clustering languages using pairwise overlap coefficients between their activation distributions.

💡 Why it matters

Testing across two mLLMs and two held-out corpora demonstrates that this identifier more effectively isolates language-specific causal effects. This results in:

  • Up to 4.9$×$ higher on-target language damage per neuron.
  • Preservation of off-target language performance.

#mLLM #LanguageModels #NeuralNetworks #NLP

Source: Distribution-aware Language Neuron Identification in Multilingual Large Language Models

item.title: Cantonese-Specific Training Improves Language Model Fit to Eye-Tracking Data
item.description:
Cantonese-Specific Training Improves Language Model Fit to Eye-Tracking Data

Information-theoretic measures derived from autoregressive language models are widely used to characterize the expectations that shape human reading, but whether language-variety-specific training improves such psycholinguistic alignment remains unclear.

This question is still open for Cantonese, where recent NLP evaluations reported mixed benefits from Cantonese-specific training relative to Mandarin-oriented or general-purpose models.

🔍 Overview

Information-theoretic measures derived from autoregressive language models are widely used to characterize the expectations that shape human reading, but whether language-variety-specific training improves such psycholinguistic alignment remains unclear.

This question is still open for Cantonese, where recent NLP evaluations reported mixed benefits from Cantonese-specific training relative to Mandarin-oriented or general-purpose models.

🧩 Method

Using naturalistic Cantonese eye-tracking data, we compare two within-family adaptation contrasts: CKIP GPT-2 Tiny versus its lightly Cantonese-adapted JED351 derivative, and Qwen2.5-7B versus CantoneseLLM-7B, which underwent substantially more extensive Cantonese continued pretraining and instruction tuning.

From each model, we derive lexical surprisal, POS surprisal, entropy before the target, and entropy reduction.

  • lexical surprisal
  • POS surprisal
  • entropy before the target
  • entropy reduction
Model Training adaptation
CKIP GPT-2 Tiny CKIP GPT-2 Tiny
JED351 its lightly Cantonese-adapted JED351 derivative
Qwen2.5-7B Qwen2.5-7B
CantoneseLLM-7B CantoneseLLM-7B, which underwent substantially more extensive Cantonese continued pretraining and instruction tuning

📊 Findings

Lexical surprisal and the joint four-metric model consistently favor CantoneseLLM-7B, followed by Qwen2.5-7B, CKIP, and JED351, whereas entropy reduction favors CKIP.

These results suggest that more extensive Cantonese-specific training can be associated with stronger predictive fit, while model rankings also depend on the information-theoretic measure being evaluated.

item.title: Time Travel Through Text: Teaching AI to Write Like It's 1840
item.description:
🍀 Time Travel Through Text: Teaching AI to Write Like It’s 1840

Summary: Discover how to transform modern AI language models into 19th-century Irish wordsmiths through an innovative style transfer technique combining reinforcement learning with historical text patterns. This practical experiment shows how to create specialized language models that can adopt distinctive writing styles without extensive manual training data.

🔮 When Old Meets New: The AI Time Machine

Have you ever wondered what would happen if modern AI could write like a 19th-century Irish periodical? That’s exactly what this fascinating experiment explores by teaching a language model to mimic the distinctive, verbose style of the Irish Penny Journal from 1840.

Picture this: instead of the concise, straightforward text generation we’re accustomed to from modern LLMs, we get flowery prose filled with antiquated expressions and verbose constructions that transport us to another era. Not just as a party trick, but as a technical demonstration of 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘴𝘵𝘺𝘭𝘦 𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘴𝘧𝘦𝘳 can work in practice!

🧠 The Technical Magic Behind Style Transfer

This experiment leverages three key technical components to achieve its time-traveling text generation:

1️⃣ Smart Dataset Creation

Instead of collecting massive amounts of training data, the approach uses a semi-synthetic dataset with a brilliant twist. The positive examples come from actual Irish Penny Journal texts, while the negative examples are the 𝘴𝘢𝘮𝘦 𝘵𝘦𝘹𝘵𝘴 rewritten in modern English using DSPy.

1
2
3
4

class IrishPennyTranslator(dspy.Signature):
 input_text: str = dspy.InputField(description="Text from Irish Penny Journal")
 cleaned_input_text: str = dspy.OutputField(description="Cleaned original text")
 modernized_text: str = dspy.OutputField(description="Translation to modern (US) English")

This pairing ensures the model learns stylistic differences rather than simply focusing on historical concepts, resulting in about 4,000 paired examples without requiring manual annotation.

2️⃣ Lightweight Style Classification

Rather than using a massive model, a tiny but effective classifier based on MiniLMv2 (just 22MB!) was trained to distinguish between Irish Penny Journal style and modern English. The binary classifier achieved 99% accuracy in minutes, proving that style recognition doesn’t require enormous computational resources.

3️⃣ 🔥 Reinforcement Learning with GRPO

The real magic happens in the application of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a reinforcement learning technique that:

  • Doesn’t require a separate critic model (saving VRAM)
  • Works well with memory-saving techniques like LoRA adapters
  • Can run on consumer hardware

The trained classifier becomes a reward model, calculating advantages by comparing individual responses to the group mean:

𝗔̂ᵢₜ = 𝗥(𝗾, 𝗼ᵢ) - 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻{𝗥(𝗾, 𝗼₁), …, 𝗥(𝗾, 𝗼ₙ)}

This steers the model toward generating text that scores higher on “Irish Penny Journal-ness” over multiple training iterations.

📜 The Results: AI’s Victorian Voice

After training, the model transforms from standard modern AI responses to something quite extraordinary. When asked about how it feels after training, it responds with delightful Victorian verbosity:

“Alas! I am but an artificial entity, devoid of the mortal joys and tribulations that beset thy human kin. Yet, in my virtual realm, I may attempt to elucidate the sensations of those who partake in such physical trials.”

The language features distinctive hallmarks of 19th-century writing:

  • Archaic grammar and vocabulary (“thy,” “beset,” “elucidate”)
  • Dramatic, philosophical reflections
  • Extended metaphors and references to mythology
  • Formal address to the reader

All this emerged not from direct imitation but through reinforcement learning guided by a tiny classifier!

🚀 Why This Matters for AI Development

This experiment demonstrates something incredibly valuable for AI development: 𝗽𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝘁𝘆𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗲𝗿 without massive datasets or computational resources.

The implications extend far beyond Victorian prose:

  • 🎯 Targeted Personality Development: Create AI with specific personas for different applications
  • 🔄 Adaptable Tone: Train models to match brand voices or specialized communication styles
  • 🌍 Cultural Context: Develop AI that can communicate in culturally specific ways
  • 📊 Efficient Training: Achieve specialized results without massive computational resources

The approach shows how carefully designed reward functions combined with strategic dataset creation can enable highly specialized AI behavior without the computational costs typically associated with large-scale model training.

💭 Final Thoughts: The Future of AI Personalization

This experiment shows us that AI personality isn’t just about what information systems contain, but 𝘩𝘰𝘸 they express it. By teaching a model to write in a distinctive historical style, we glimpse a future where AI communication could be infinitely customizable.

The next time you interact with an AI, consider not just what it knows, but how it tells you what it knows. Could your digital assistant speak like Shakespeare? Write like Hemingway? Or perhaps converse like an 1840s Irish periodical?

As AI development continues, perhaps the most human quality we can give these systems isn’t just knowledge, but style—the distinctive voice that makes communication uniquely engaging. What voice would you want your AI to speak with?

item.title: Breaking Ethical Ground: Common Pile & Comma Models Prove You Don't Need to Steal Data
item.description:
🚀 Breaking Ethical Ground: Common Pile & Comma Models Prove You Don’t Need to Steal Data

📊 Summary

The Hugging Face team has released Common Pile v0.1, an 8TB dataset of legally sound, openly licensed text spanning 30 diverse sources. To prove its efficacy, they’ve trained two 7B parameter language models (Comma v0.1-1T and v0.1-2T) that compete with major models trained on questionable data. This breakthrough challenges the industry assumption that powerful AI requires ethically dubious training materials.

🌟 Ethical AI: No Longer Just a Dream

For years, the AI community has wrestled with an uncomfortable truth: many of the most powerful language models are trained on vast amounts of text scraped from the internet with little regard for copyright, licensing, or consent. The question lingering in researchers’ minds has been whether it’s even possible to build competitive models without resorting to these ethically questionable practices.

Today, we have our answer. And it’s a resounding “yes.” 🙌

The release of the Common Pile v0.1 dataset and accompanying Comma models represents a watershed moment in AI development. This project demonstrates that ethical considerations and technical excellence aren’t mutually exclusive—they can and should coexist.

🧠 What Makes the Common Pile Special?

Diverse, Legal, and Massive

The Common Pile isn’t just another dataset—it’s an 𝟴 𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗯𝘆𝘁𝗲 collection carefully curated from 30 distinct sources, all adhering to proper licensing. This diversity ensures models trained on it develop a rich understanding across multiple domains:

  • 📚 Books and literature
  • 💻 Programming code
  • 🔬 Research papers
  • 🎓 Educational materials
  • 🎙️ Audio transcripts
  • 📜 Governmental text
  • …and much more

The team behind Common Pile has prioritized legal and ethical sourcing, using only openly licensed and public domain text. This stands in stark contrast to many existing datasets that incorporate copyrighted materials without permission or proper attribution.

A Foundation for Ethical Models

The dataset wasn’t created merely as an academic exercise—it was designed with practical application in mind. The creators posed a fundamental question: “𝙄𝙨 𝙞𝙩 𝙥𝙤𝙨𝙨𝙞𝙗𝙡𝙚 𝙩𝙤 𝙩𝙧𝙖𝙞𝙣 𝙥𝙚𝙧𝙛𝙤𝙧𝙢𝙖𝙣𝙩 𝙡𝙖𝙣𝙜𝙪𝙖𝙜𝙚 𝙢𝙤𝙙𝙚𝙡𝙨 𝙬𝙞𝙩𝙝𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙪𝙨𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙪𝙣𝙡𝙞𝙘𝙚𝙣𝙨𝙚𝙙 𝙩𝙚𝙭𝙩?”

🔥 The Comma Models: Proving the Concept

To answer their own question, the team trained two language models on the Common Pile:

  • Comma v0.1-1T: A 7B parameter model trained on 1 trillion tokens
  • Comma v0.1-2T: A 7B parameter model trained on 2 trillion tokens

The results? 🤯 Nothing short of revolutionary. These models achieve competitive performance compared to similar-sized models like Llama 1 and 2 7B—models trained on data of questionable provenance.

This achievement shatters the persistent myth that cutting ethical corners is necessary to build powerful AI systems. The Comma models demonstrate that with careful curation and proper engineering, ethically sourced data can produce results that rival or potentially exceed those of less scrupulous approaches.

Technical Details That Matter

The team didn’t just release the models—they’ve provided complete transparency into their process:

  • ✅ Full model checkpoints available for download
  • ✅ Access to the filtered and rebalanced dataset used for training
  • ✅ Open-source code for data preparation on GitHub
  • ✅ Comprehensive documentation in their research paper

This level of openness sets a new standard for the field, allowing others to build upon their work and potentially improve these ethical approaches further.

🌈 The Future of Ethical AI

The “v0.1” designation in the project’s name isn’t accidental—it’s a clear signal that this is just the beginning. The team views this release as the first step on a longer journey toward building a more ethical language model ecosystem.

What might future versions include? We might see:

  • Expanded datasets with even greater diversity
  • Improved filtering techniques to ensure higher quality
  • More sophisticated balancing methods to reduce biases
  • Models of various sizes to accommodate different use cases
  • Community contributions to enhance the dataset’s breadth and depth

This collaborative approach to ethical AI development could fundamentally transform how we think about building these systems, proving that the AI community doesn’t need to compromise on ethics to achieve technical excellence.

🤔 A Paradigm Shift in AI Development

The Common Pile and Comma models don’t just represent technical achievements—they represent a potential paradigm shift in how we approach AI development. By demonstrating that competitive models can be built using exclusively ethical data sources, the team has challenged the entire industry to reconsider its practices.

For too long, many have assumed that cutting corners on data ethics was the price of progress. The Comma models suggest otherwise: perhaps the truly advanced approach is one that respects copyright, licensing, and the fundamental principles of ethical data usage.

As AI becomes increasingly integrated into our daily lives, the methods used to create these systems matter more than ever. The Common Pile project offers a glimpse of a future where powerful AI and ethical considerations advance hand-in-hand.

💡 What’s Next?

If you’re intrigued by this project (and you should be!), there are several ways to engage:

  1. Explore the dataset and models firsthand
  2. Review their paper for detailed methodology and results
  3. Open an issue on GitHub if you have ideas for improvement
  4. Reach out directly to the team to collaborate

As we stand at this ethical crossroads in AI development, one question remains: will the industry follow this lead and embrace methods that respect both legal and ethical considerations, or will it continue down the path of “scrape first, ask questions later”? The answer may determine not just how our AI systems perform, but what values they ultimately embody.

item.title: DeepSeek R1-0528: The Reasoning Powerhouse Distilled to a Compact 8B Model
item.description:
🚀 DeepSeek R1-0528: The Reasoning Powerhouse Distilled to a Compact 8B Model

📊 Summary

DeepSeek’s latest R1-0528 model makes significant leaps in reasoning abilities, matching top models like O3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro in mathematical and programming tasks. Most impressively, they’ve distilled this reasoning power into an 8B parameter model that outperforms competitors twice its size. This blog explores the technical improvements, evaluation results, and how you can run this reasoning powerhouse locally.

🧠 The Evolution of AI Reasoning: DeepSeek R1’s Quantum Leap

The quest for AI systems that can truly reason - rather than merely predict the next token - has been the holy grail of language model research. DeepSeek’s latest iteration, the R1-0528 model, represents a significant milestone in this journey, showcasing remarkable improvements in deep reasoning capabilities.

What makes this update particularly noteworthy isn’t just incremental improvement but a fundamental enhancement in how the model approaches complex problems. The R1-0528 demonstrates substantially improved mathematical reasoning, programming abilities, and general logical inference - approaching capabilities previously seen only in heavyweight proprietary models.

📸 Imagine a comparison chart showing the evolution of token usage in reasoning tasks between versions

The most striking evidence of this improvement comes from standardized mathematical tests. On the AIME 2025 test, accuracy jumped from 70% to an impressive 87.5%. How? By dramatically increasing reasoning depth - the model now uses nearly twice as many tokens per question (23K vs 12K) to work through complex problems step by step.

🔍 Breaking Down the Benchmark Results

The performance metrics tell a compelling story about R1-0528’s capabilities across different domains:

𝗠𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 👨‍🔬

  • AIME 2024: 91.4% (up from 79.8%)
  • AIME 2025: 87.5% (up from 70.0%)
  • HMMT 2025: 79.4% (up from 41.7% - nearly doubling performance!)

These numbers represent more than just statistical improvements. The model is now approaching human expert-level performance on some of the most challenging mathematical competitions designed for gifted high school students.

𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 💻

  • LiveCodeBench: 73.3% (up from 63.5%)
  • Codeforces-Div1 Rating: 1930 (up from 1530)
  • SWE Verified: 57.6% (up from 49.2%)

The rating improvement on Codeforces is particularly significant - a 400-point jump represents crossing from intermediate to advanced competitive programming ability.

🔥 The 8B Parameter Miracle: Small Package, Big Reasoning

Perhaps the most revolutionary aspect of DeepSeek’s announcement is the R1-0528-Qwen3-8B model. This compact 8B-parameter model achieves what was previously thought impossible: matching or exceeding the performance of much larger models on complex reasoning tasks.

By distilling the chain-of-thought reasoning patterns from the full DeepSeek-R1-0528 model into Qwen3’s 8B architecture, the team has created what might be the most efficient reasoning model in the open-source landscape.

📸 Imagine a visual comparison showing the model size vs. performance tradeoff

Consider these remarkable comparisons:

  • DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B achieves 86.0% on AIME 2024
  • This outperforms Qwen3-8B by +10.0%
  • It matches the performance of Qwen3-235B-thinking (a model ~30x larger!)
  • It even beats Gemini-2.5-Flash-Thinking-0520 on this benchmark

This represents a significant breakthrough in model efficiency. The ability to run sophisticated reasoning capabilities on consumer hardware opens up possibilities for developers and researchers who don’t have access to enterprise-grade computing infrastructure.

⚙️ Running DeepSeek R1-0528 Models Locally

Want to experience these reasoning capabilities firsthand? The implementation is surprisingly straightforward:

𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗢𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗺𝗮 𝗨𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘀: 

1

ollama run hf.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B-GGUF:Q4_K_XL

This command automatically sets the appropriate chat template and configurations.

𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀:

  • Temperature: 0.6 (recommended, range 0.5-0.7)
  • Top_P value: 0.95

The chat template follows this format:

1

<｜begin▁of▁sentence｜><｜User｜>What is 1+1?<｜Assistant｜>It's 2.<｜end▁of▁sentence｜><｜User｜>Explain more!<｜Assistant｜>

🔔 Key improvements in the new version:

  • System prompts are now supported
  • You no longer need to add “\n” at the beginning to trigger reasoning patterns

For those looking to experiment with the 8B model, note that while its architecture is identical to Qwen3-8B, it uses DeepSeek-R1-0528’s tokenizer configuration. Ensure you source all configuration files from the DeepSeek repository rather than the original Qwen3 project.

🤔 What This Means for AI Development

The progress demonstrated by DeepSeek R1-0528 - particularly its successful distillation into an 8B model - has profound implications for the field:

  1. Democratization of AI reasoning: Advanced reasoning capabilities can now run on consumer hardware, opening new possibilities for developers with limited resources.

  2. Academic research boost: The chain-of-thought knowledge transfer demonstrated could accelerate research into more efficient reasoning models.

  3. Industrial applications: Small-scale models with powerful reasoning abilities could enable new edge applications where computation is constrained but complex decision-making is required.

The MIT License under which these models are released further enhances their impact, supporting both commercial use and further distillation experiments.

🌟 Conclusion: The Rise of Efficient Reasoning

DeepSeek’s R1-0528 series represents a significant step toward AI systems that can truly reason rather than just predict. The full model’s improvements are impressive enough, but the successful distillation of these capabilities into an 8B parameter model may prove to be the more revolutionary achievement.

As these models continue to evolve, we may see a fundamental shift in what’s possible with consumer-grade AI. Could the next breakthrough come from further optimizing these reasoning patterns, or will we need entirely new architectures to take the next leap forward?

item.title: Slashing Memory by 40%: How Liger GRPO Revolutionizes Language Model Fine-Tuning
item.description:
🐯 Slashing Memory by 40%: How Liger GRPO Revolutionizes Language Model Fine-Tuning

📌 𝙎𝙪𝙢𝙢𝙖𝙧𝙮

Liger now supercharges TRL’s Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) Trainer with a remarkable 40% reduction in memory usage without sacrificing model quality. This technical breakthrough also brings full FSDP and PEFT support, making it easier than ever to scale reinforcement learning across multiple GPUs for language model fine-tuning.

🚀 Reinforcement Learning for Language Models: Evolution Not Revolution

Fine-tuning language models with reinforcement learning has traditionally been a resource-intensive endeavor. The standard approach—Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)—demands significant computational resources, requiring multiple models to be loaded into memory simultaneously: policy, value, reward, and reference models.

The emergence of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been a game-changer, particularly with DeepSeek’s R1 model demonstrating its effectiveness. Unlike traditional RLHF, GRPO eliminates the need for pre-trained reward and value models, instead leveraging 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 that can directly check output correctness without external reward models.

📸 See illustration above comparing GRPO vs PPO training pipelines

However, even with these improvements, reinforcement learning for language models remained memory-hungry—until now.

💾 The Memory Optimization Magic: How Liger Kernel Works

The breakthrough lies in extending Liger’s Chunked Loss approach to the GRPO Loss calculation. This elegant solution avoids storing full logits in memory during each training step, which is typically a major contributor to peak memory usage when dealing with large vocabularies, extensive sequence lengths, or substantial batch sizes.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀:

  1. The input to the lm_head is chunked across the batch dimension
  2. Forward pass is executed one chunk at a time
  3. Gradients for each loss chunk are calculated during the forward pass
  4. These gradients are accumulated progressively through each chunk

This isn’t just a minor optimization—it’s a fundamental rethinking of how memory is managed during training. The typical approach would still require all logits to be stored in GPU memory for the backward pass, but Liger’s implementation calculates gradients with respect to input chunks and lm_head weights during the forward pass itself.

📸 See visualization of the optimization process in the diagram above

🔌 Plug-and-Play Integration with TRL

The best part? Implementation is remarkably straightforward. With the integration of Liger GRPO into TRL (PR #3184), enabling these memory savings requires just a single parameter change:

1

training_args = GRPOConfig(output_dir="Qwen3-0.6B-GRPO", use_liger_loss=True)

Once you’ve installed TRL from source using:

1

pip install "trl[liger] @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/trl.git"

The full implementation is just a few lines of code away:

from trl import GRPOConfig, GRPOTrainer
from datasets import load_dataset

train_dataset = load_dataset("trl-lib/tldr", split="train")
training_args = GRPOConfig(output_dir="Qwen3-0.6B-GRPO", use_liger_loss=True)

def reward_len(completions, **kwargs):
 return [-abs(20 - len(completion)) for completion in completions]

trainer = GRPOTrainer(
 model="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Instruct",
 reward_funcs=reward_len,
 args=training_args,
 train_dataset=train_dataset,
)
trainer.train()

🚂 Scaling to New Heights: FSDP, PEFT, and vLLM Integration

Taking things further, Liger GRPO Loss now supports Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP) and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), opening doors to distributed training across multiple GPUs or nodes.

The PEFT integration is particularly clever, as techniques like LoRA and QLoRA reduce memory requirements by only tuning smaller adapter weights. An added bonus: using PEFT with GRPO eliminates the need to load a separate reference model—you can access the original, unmodified model during training by simply disabling the LoRA adapters.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲:

  • 1.5x to 1.8x increase in maximum possible batch size
  • Seamless scaling across different Qwen3 model sizes

For even greater acceleration, Liger Loss integrates with TRL’s vLLM server for faster text generation during training. This three-step setup process is straightforward:

  1. 🚀 Start the vLLM server on a dedicated GPU
  2. 🔧 Configure your training script with use_vllm=True
  3. 🏃‍♂️ Launch training on a different GPU

With the memory efficiency of Liger-GRPO, combined with FSDP and PEFT support, fine-tuning language models using reinforcement learning is finally becoming accessible to researchers and developers with limited GPU resources.
